01 Case study

Dynamic Bank Statement Mapping

Designing a flexible system for importing and interpreting changing bank statement formats

CompanyFintranet ↗ · LinkedIn ↗
ProductFintraAccount ↗
IndustryB2B fintech for money service businesses

FintraAccount is a multi-currency accounting platform where bank statement transactions can be imported as structured financial Activities.

I designed a configurable mapping system that enables different statement structures to be translated into FintraAccount’s financial model — while keeping recurring imports simple and financial data traceable.

  • ConfigurableNew structures are set up without engineering work.
  • TraceableEvery transaction links to its file, batch, template and version.
  • ValidatedInvalid files are stopped before they create Activities.
  • ExtensibleAI mapping and Open Banking can be added without reworking the model.

In brief

The problemEvery new or changed bank statement format meant engineering work and a release. It did not scale.
The solutionA system where users define the mapping themselves: they create a template, match the file's columns to FintraAccount's fixed fields, and reuse it on every import.
My partAs the solo Product Designer I proposed this approach and designed it end to end, from information architecture to validation, ready for development.

Key terms

ActivityOne transaction record in FintraAccount, created from a statement row or entered manually.
Money EntityA bank account in FintraAccount.
InstitutionThe bank (called PSP in the older version) that owns a set of statement templates.
Template and versionA template is one statement format of a bank, with its mapping. A version is one saved configuration of it.
General TemplateA built-in, fixed template users can fill by hand. It has no versions.

The problem

Supporting a new statement format depended on the engineering team.

FintraAccount could import bank statements, but support relied on predefined formats. As institutions and formats changed, the same type of request could repeatedly return to Product, Design and Engineering. At times a request to add a new bank statement or change an existing format arrived only two days after the previous one, and after one wave of bank changes around ten formats needed support at once.

The system worked — but the way it adapted did not scale.

For customers. Wait for a release before a new format works.
For the team. Recurring design and engineering capacity spent on variations of the same problem.
For Product. Scaling to more clients and banks became increasingly difficult as statement formats evolved.
How might we make statement support configurable enough to adapt to changing formats, while keeping everyday imports simple and financial data reliable?

Understanding the variability

What actually changes between statements, and what doesn't.

I reviewed close to 30 statement formats: around 15 from the bank accounts of the exchange house FintraAccount was built for, and the rest benchmarked myself. Some columns repeated across almost every statement; others appeared in only a few.

Even data that every statement shared, like the amount, was shown in different ways: one signed column, separate debit and credit columns, a Dr/Cr marker, commas or points as decimals, a currency inside the amount. Dates varied down to the calendar: the exchange house's Iranian banks report solar-calendar dates while the app worked in Gregorian, and users corrected dates by hand.

Two things came out of this

A catalog of fields

The same meanings kept returning, so I defined the Statement Field Catalog: the fixed set of fields FintraAccount understands.

RequiredDate and timeDebit and credit amountsCurrency…OptionalActivity IDPayment referenceCounterparty…Statement-level, stored on the Import BatchOpening balancePeriod…

Same data, different shapes

A field can be common to every statement and still be written differently. The catalog says what a field means; rules say how to read it. That led to transformation rules, introduced later.

-1,250.00Debit 1,250.001.250,00 EUR
→
Amount 1250.00
Direction: debit
Currency: EUR
FintraAccount didn't need to know every format. It needed a way to translate them.

Constraints that shaped the solution

Flexibility couldn't compromise financial reliability or everyday usability.

Financial integrityAn incorrect mapping creates incorrect financial records.
Historical traceabilityChanging a configuration must never change how earlier imports are understood.
Two complexity budgetsSetup is rare and done by administrators. Importing is daily. Configuration lives in Settings.
Don't disturb what worksActivity creation, allocation and the General Template import stay unchanged.
Room to growThe model translates financial data; it isn't tied to CSV upload.
No direct access to usersI worked from the Product Owner's feedback and past customer behaviour.

The reframe

From supporting bank formats to translating financial structures.

The solution: let the user define the mapping

Before, our team had to translate each bank's statement into FintraAccount's internal structure every time a bank was added or changed. I proposed a different approach: let the user do this translation, and I designed the whole system around it.

FintraAccount has a fixed set of fields for a bank Activity, defined from the field catalog. The user creates a template for a statement format and matches the columns of a sample file to those fields. This is what we call mapping. Later, when importing, the user picks the template and the system uses its mapping to bring the data in.

BeforeBank statement→Our team writes the translation in code→FintraAccount
NowBank statement→Template: a mapping the user defines once→FintraAccount
1. Fixed fieldsFintraAccount defines the fields of a bank Activity, based on the field catalog.
2. Map onceThe user creates a template and matches the columns of a sample file to those fields.
3. Import with the templateAt import the user chooses the template and the system applies its mapping.
External structures can change. Internal financial meaning should remain stable.

Mapping starts from a suggestion. When the user uploads a file while creating a template, the system extracts its columns. It compares them with the system fields, using a table I prepared of the names each field usually appears under, plus what it learns from how users correct it. Columns it recognises are mapped automatically; the ones it can't are left unmapped. Either way, the user can change everything. The AI only suggests: it makes the user faster and more accurate without limiting them. We planned it for the second iteration.

The user stays in charge. Every mapping can be changed, whether suggested or not.Auto-mappedManualNot mapped

How the model evolved

I started from the problem, and the structure followed one question at a time.

Where should mapping templates live?

Once mapping became dynamic, users needed somewhere to create their templates. My first thought was the bank's Money Entity. But one bank can have several accounts, and each would need the same template built again. So I moved templates one level up, to the bank itself: the Institution, called PSP in the old system.

There was nothing to build on. Institutions existed only as a seeded list: when creating a bank Money Entity, the user picked a PSP from it, and nobody could manage that list. So Institution management had to come first. I designed it as a minimal MVP that can scale, then spent the main effort on templates and mapping inside it, and finally on how they affect the bank Money Entity and the import.

Decision. Institutions became a managed entity that owns templates; a Money Entity only references one.

What happens when a format changes?

Editing a template in place would rewrite how past imports are interpreted, so versions are immutable. Because banks usually change a statement incrementally, I added Clone Version: copy any existing version and change only what differs. The copy is saved as a new, latest version, and the existing ones are never touched.

Who chooses the version at import?

My first design let users pick the version. After discussing it with the Product Owner and how rarely an older version is needed, I removed the choice: imports always use the Current Version. Importing a statement in an old format is a rare edge case; it can be entered manually, or imported by cloning the old version and then cloning the current one again.

How flexible should mapping be?

I explored conditional rules and documented the research in a user story. They add configuration, validation and maintenance cost, so I chose a fixed field catalog with predefined rules, leaving room for richer ones later.

No ruleSome fields need none. The Rule column shows N/A, as for activity date and time, whose format is already set at file level.
Set by the systemSome fields have a rule the system defines. The user can't change it, only read it: statement currency comes from the Money Entity, and reconciliation fields default to the statement values.
Chosen by the userFor debit and credit amounts the user picks from a few rules, such as Direct Mapping or Negative = Debit. “Direction decides debit/credit” appears only when two source columns are selected, and is then fixed. Every choice is validated.
Configurability is useful only until the cost of understanding the configuration becomes greater than the problem it solves.
Where do global templates live? The IA record compared three options and chose a separate area. The user stories then settled on one built-in General Template with no versions, because it follows FintraAccount's own Activity fields, not any bank.
Where does Institution Management live? In Settings: it is administration, not daily financial work.

The final system

Two lanes with different complexity: set up once in Settings, import every day.

Everything starts on the Institution page in Settings, where a bank's templates and versions live. Administrators set up templates there. Accounting and operations users import statements from their bank's Money Entity, and the system applies the template's mapping.

Setup: administrators, in Settings

InstitutionThe bank, managed in Settings
TemplateOne statement format of that bank
VersionOne configuration; the latest is the Current Version
Mapping and rulesWhich column goes to which field, and how it is read

Daily import: accounting and operations users

Money EntityThe bank account being imported
Choose templateGeneral, or one of the institution's
Upload fileThe latest version is applied
ValidateRules checked; any failure stops the import
PreviewWhat will enter, before it does
ImportActivities created, linked to a batch

Setting up a template

In the product this is a three-step wizard: template info and upload, map columns, review and validation. Underneath, five things happen.

Step 1

Upload a sample file

The user names the template, picks the bank and uploads a sample file. The system analyses it, reports the sheet, the number of columns and the header row, and extracts every column. Nothing is imported at this point.

Step 2

Describe how the file writes dates

Before mapping, the user sets the time zone, the calendar type (solar or Gregorian) and the date and time format. If a field has no time, the system uses 09:00:00. This answers the calendar problem found in the research: dates are converted to the internal standard on import, so nobody fixes them by hand.

Step 3

Match columns to fields

System fields are listed on one side, required ones marked with a star. Each gets a file column from a dropdown, and a badge shows how it was mapped: Auto-mapped, Manual or Not mapped. A side panel tracks which columns are used and which are left, and a Preview column shows at once what the value will look like. Statement-level fields, such as balances and period, are mapped in their own block.

Step 4

Choose how each field is read

Some data is the same everywhere but written differently, so a rule tells the system how to read it. The amount is the clearest case: banks show it in five common shapes, and each one ends up in the same two fields, debit amount and credit amount. Rules also protect the data by failing rows that make no sense.

Step 5

Review, validate, publish

Before publishing, the user sees a summary: required fields mapped (for example 7 of 7), optional fields mapped, columns left unmapped, and a sample of the first rows as the system will store them. Publishing is blocked until every required mapping is complete. Once published, the template is ready for every future import.

Importing, day to day

Importing is the small part. The user opens the bank's Money Entity, picks the General Template or one of the institution's templates, and uploads the file. The system validates it, shows a preview of what will enter, and imports. The latest version is always used, so there is nothing to configure.

Most complexity lives in configuration. Once a template is ready, the recurring experience stays small.

Keeping imports trustworthy

Validation. Publishing a template is blocked until its required mappings are complete. At import, errors block the whole file: the user sees how many records are invalid and can expand a row to see exactly what is wrong. Duplicates, matched by Activity ID, are treated differently: they are flagged and skipped, and the rest of the file can still be imported.

Traceability. Each file creates one Import Batch. From any Activity, a user sees the source document, batch, template and version, and the original statement row.

Designing through feasibility

Feasibility was part of the design loop, not a final checkpoint.

  • Version choice. Changed after a conversation with the Product Owner.
  • Versioning. Historical imports must reference the configuration used then, so versions are immutable.
  • Ownership. Mapping is reusable without duplication, so templates belong to institutions.
  • Existing rules. All-or-nothing import and duplicate detection already existed; I made failures explicit.
  • Batch, file and row. Linking each imported Activity to its import batch, its file and the exact file row, and to the template and version that interpreted it, needed a conversation with engineering. Once we were sure how it would be built, it went into the design and the final decisions.

Because these conversations ran throughout, the team was already onboarded on the feature at handoff.

Where it landed

System modelInstitutions, templates, versions
MappingField catalog, rules, wizard
ValidationFormats, currencies, duplicates
DeliveryFlows, high-fidelity UI, three user stories

The design was completed and handed over to development. Post-release metrics weren't available, so what follows describes what the system was designed to enable, not measured results.

  • Less engineering dependency. A new compatible format becomes configuration, not a release.
  • Safe evolution. v1, v2 and v3 without rewriting history.
  • Simpler daily work. Upload, validate, preview, import.
  • Ready to extend. AI mapping and Open Banking reuse the same translation principle.

How I would measure it: format requests still needing engineering, time from request to first successful import, import failure rate by category, and how often users accept AI suggestions.

What I took forward

A small request revealed a system problem.

I started from one request, support another format, and found the larger need behind it. The hardest part was balancing a complete feature against a simple one: every decision came down to where the complexity should live. What I am proudest of is how complete the handoff was: flows, validation, field rules and user stories were all ready, and the team was already onboarded when it happened.

When a workflow keeps getting complicated, I first question the product model behind it before trying to simplify the screens.

Open questions: a better duplicate detection strategy and governance of the General Template. Next: build AI-assisted mapping, then test the model against real Open Banking payloads.
